newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Conservatives try to get out of EMU hole.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Conservatives try to get out of EMU hole.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke braced on Monday for a bid to defuse a row over Europe that has reopened gaping divisions in the ruling Conservative party less than six months before an election.

Clarke was making a statement to parliament (eds: 1530 GMT) to try to placate Conservative "Eurosceptics" furious at what they suspect is an attempt by ministers to stifle debate over rules governing the European Union's planned single currency.

The Treasury said Clarke wanted to correct "misleading reports" in the press suggesting Britain could be bound by any decisions on economic and monetary union (EMU) taken by EU finance ministers and heads of government next month.
Britain negotiated an opt-out from EMU in 1991 and Prime Minister John Major has postponed any decision on Britain's membership until after the election.
The timing of the statement is extraordinary, coming just 24 hours before Clarke unveils his annual budget.

Conservatives regard the budget, expected to include tax cuts and a bullish assessment of Britain's economic prospects, as the party's best remaining hope of clawing back the big lead the opposition Labour Party holds in opinion polls. A general election must be held by May 22.

Party officials said Major agreed to the statement out of concern that the rumbling row over whether parliament should be given a chance to debate three dense working papers on EMU was overshadowing the budget.
Eurosceptics fiercely opposed to closer European ties welcomed the chance to voice their concerns to Clarke, a leading pro-European.

"What I wanted was an opportunity for myself and colleagues to be able to ask the Chancellor (finance minister) questions and expose the issues before he signs up to anything at the (EU) finance ministers' meeting. Timing was most important," John Redwood, a prominent Conservative right-winger, told BBC radio.

Redwood and other Eurosceptics are worried that the working papers, though technical, mark another step on a road leading sooner or later to Britain's participation in the single currency, due to be launched in January 1999.

Momentum toward EMU was boosted on Monday when Italy rejoined the EU's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), four years after it was forced out by speculators. Only Britain, Sweden and Greece now remain outside the ERM, a staging post for EMU.

European Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan reassured sceptical Conservatives that Britain would not be bound by a proposed stability pact under which EMU members who run up big budget deficits would be fined.
But the rules were needed to make the single currency work effectively, Brittan, a former Conservative minister, said.

"Britain has an interest in making it work properly, in ensuring it is sensible, even though there is no way whatsoever, by any distortion, trick or any sleight of hand, by which this could be imposed on Britain unless Britain voluntarily decides to join the EMU," Brittan told BBC radio.
